title: Who Has Gone Up to Heaven?
sum: Chapter 30 belongs to Agur son of Jakeh, a sage known from nowhere else. He opens not with advice but with a confession: he is more beast than man and has no wisdom. Then he asks the questions no human can answer: who has gone up to heaven, held the wind and water, and set the ends of the earth? His answer is not his own insight but God's tested word (30:5–6), and he prays for honesty and for just enough bread (30:7–9).

The rest of the chapter is a string of sayings, most of them counted: "three things... four". They look at the world with wonder and humor: things that are never satisfied, ways too marvelous to grasp, upstarts that make the earth shake, small animals that are wise, creatures that walk with a swagger. The chapter ends where it began, with a call to put a hand over one's mouth (30:32).
readings: Agur's confession is humility before God. Human wisdom cannot climb to heaven, so the wise person trusts God's word and asks only for what he needs. Most Jewish and Christian readers have read the chapter this way, and the quotation of a psalm in 30:5 and of Deuteronomy in 30:6 supports it.

Some critics hear in 30:1–4 a skeptic, weary of God and doubting that anyone can know him, and in 30:5–6 a reply by a believing editor who quotes Scripture against him. On this reading the chapter stages a debate, like Job or Ecclesiastes, and Proverbs includes a doubter's voice before answering it. Fox discusses this view and finds the confession sincere rather than skeptical.

The chapter may be several small pieces gathered under one heading. The Greek splits it in two, placing 30:1–14 and 30:15–33 in different places (see below), which suggests that the numerical sayings once circulated apart from Agur's confession.

views.H: The heading names Agur son of Jakeh, a sage perhaps from Massa, an Arabian people descended from Ishmael (Genesis 25:14). Israel admired the wisdom of the East (1 Kings 4:30), and the book's editors preserved his words as wisdom from outside Israel, set under the God of Israel. Where his words end is not marked: some stop at 30:4, 30:9 or 30:14, others give him the whole chapter.
views.C: Critics treat chapter 30 as one of the latest additions to the book, a set of small collections. The Greek order supports this: it puts 30:1–14 after 24:22 and 30:15–33 after 24:34, and it drops the name Agur entirely, turning the heading into "Fear my words, son". The quotation of Psalm 18:30 in 30:5 and the echo of Deuteronomy 4:2 in 30:6 show an editor who knew written Scripture. Many see 30:1–9 as a deliberate frame: a sage admits the limits of wisdom near the end of a book that has praised it.
views.W: The numerical sayings have parallels at Ugarit and in the Aramaic Story of Ahiqar, and the lists of animals recall Egyptian and Mesopotamian lists of the things of the world. Egyptian texts like the Admonitions of Ipuwer describe the social order turned upside down, as in 30:21–23. Agur's questions resemble the ancient habit of teaching by riddles, and Job 38–41 is Israel's great example.
views.J: The rabbis took Agur, Jakeh and Ithiel as names of Solomon (Kohelet Rabbah 1:1). Rashi explains Agur as the one who "gathered" understanding, reads Ithiel and Ucal as "God is with me, and I will be able", and answers the question of 30:4 with Moses, who went up to God and came down with the Torah. The Talmud hears 30:2 as Solomon's repentance after his mother's rebuke (Bavli Sanhedrin 70b).
views.X: Christian readers have heard in 30:4 a hint of the Son: Augustine applied it to Christ, Matthew Henry saw the Messiah's hidden name, and Jesus' words in John 3:13 seem to answer Agur's question. Agur's prayer for daily bread (30:8) is often read beside the Lord's Prayer, and 30:5–6 has been used in debates about the sufficiency and closing of Scripture. Many commentators also warn against making 30:4 a proof text for the Trinity.

deep.h: Agur's opening line: names or a cry?
deep.b:
The first verse of chapter 30 is one of the hardest in Proverbs. Read with the vowels of the Hebrew text, it gives a heading and an address: "The words of Agur son of Jakeh, the oracle. So says the man to Ithiel, to Ithiel and Ucal." But the vowels were added centuries after the consonants, and the same letters can be divided differently. Read as la'iti 'el, la'iti 'el, wa'ekhel, they say, "I am weary, God, I am weary, God, and I am worn out." That cry would lead straight into 30:2: "Surely I am more beast than man." Many modern scholars and versions prefer it. Others propose "There is no God" or "I am not God", which would make Agur a skeptic.

The ancient translators did not read names either. The Greek has "to those who trust in God, and I stop", and Jerome's Latin, "the man with whom God is, and who, strengthened by God staying with him, said". Rashi reads "God is with me, and I will be able". The Plain English Translation keeps the names, following the Hebrew as read, and gives the alternatives in the variant at 30:1. The word "oracle" (massa') is also debated: it may be the Arabian people of Massa (see the note). Agur himself remains unknown.

deep.h: Who has gone up to heaven? Jewish and Christian readings
deep.b:
Agur's six questions in 30:4, four beginning "Who" and two beginning "What", expect the answer "no one" or "God". No human has climbed to heaven and returned with its secrets (compare Deuteronomy 30:12; Job 38). The last question, "What is his name, and what is his son's name?", has been read in at least four ways. God and his people: the one who rules wind and water is the LORD, and his son is Israel, "my son, my firstborn" (Exodus 4:22), or the king. A human expert: the question is a taunt, "name the person who knows this, and his family" (Toy, Longman). Moses: Rashi reads each question of Moses, who went up the mountain, held back the waters (Exodus 15:8) and set up the tabernacle. The Son of God: Augustine, Matthew Henry and many Christian readers since hear a hint of the eternal Son. They point to John 3:13: "Nobody has gone up into heaven except the one who came down out of heaven, the Son of Man."

The Greek reads "his children", and some scholars think of the heavenly "sons of God". In context, Agur's point is that God is beyond human reach and that his word must be trusted (30:5). Christians who read the verse of Christ usually add that this is a fuller meaning seen in the light of the New Testament, not the only one Agur's first hearers could have seen.
deep.refs: 30:4–5; Deuteronomy 30:11–14; Exodus 4:22; Exodus 15:8; John 3:13; Romans 10:6–7; Job 38:4–11

deep.b:
From 30:15 to 30:31 the chapter counts. Four sayings use the pattern "three... four" (30:15–16, 18–19, 21–23, 29–31), and one simply says "four" (30:24–28). Each sets up a riddle: what do these things share? The answers are left for the hearer: they are never satisfied; they move in ways no one can explain; they upset the order of things; they are small but wise; they walk with confidence. Short sayings are wedged between them: the leech's daughters (30:15), the eye that mocks a parent (30:17), the adulterous woman (30:20) and the warning against pride (30:32–33).

The form was old and international. Ugarit and Ahiqar have it, and so do Amos, Job, Micah and Sirach (see the topic page). It suits wisdom that watches the world: animals, the sea, the sky, the household and the court. The sayings rarely moralize. They invite wonder, and they leave the hearer to draw the lesson, which may be the point after Agur's confession that he knows nothing.

deep.h: Where the Greek puts chapters 30 and 31
deep.b:
The Greek translation of Proverbs, made in Egypt in the 200s or 100s BC, has the same material as the Hebrew at the end of the book but in a different order, and without the names of Agur and Lemuel:

Hebrew order (and English Bibles)Greek order (Rahlfs)Swete's numbering (Codex Vaticanus)
22:17–24:22, the words of the wise22:17–24:22, with five extra lines (24:22a–e)22:17–24:22, with additions (24:22a–e)
30:1–14, Agur's wordsplaced after 24:2224:24–37
24:23–34, more sayings of the wiseplaced after 30:1424:38–49
30:15–33, the numerical sayingsplaced after 24:3424:50–68
31:1–9, Lemuel's motherplaced after 30:3324:69–77
25:1–29:27, Hezekiah's collectionfollows 31:925:1–29:27
31:10–31, the woman of strengthplaced after 29:27, at the end29:28–49

In Swete's edition the Hebrew 30:1 is numbered 24:24, right after the additions 24:22a–e. So in the Greek the words of Agur and Lemuel sit inside "the words of the wise", and Hezekiah's collection is followed directly by the woman of strength, which closes the book as it does in Hebrew. Because the headings with Agur's and Lemuel's names have become ordinary sentences in the Greek ("Fear my words, son"; "My words have been spoken by God"), the whole book reads as Solomon's. Scholars disagree about the cause. Emanuel Tov and others think the translator had a Hebrew text arranged differently, an earlier edition of the book's last chapters. Johann Cook and others think the Greek translator or an early editor rearranged it. Either way, the order shows that 30:1–14, 30:15–33, 31:1–9 and 31:10–31 once circulated as separate pieces.

The Plain English Translation is made from the Leningrad Codex (AD 1008), read word by word, with the Masoretes' notes on words written one way and read another (Ketiv and Qere) at 30:10, 30:18, 31:4, 31:16 and 31:18. The Greek was checked directly in Rahlfs's edition, and Codex Vaticanus in Swete's edition, whose notes give the readings of Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus and Ephraemi. Jerome's Latin (the Vulgate) was checked for selected verses. The Syriac and the Targum were not checked directly, and the notes do not cite them.

The Dead Sea Scrolls have nothing of these chapters. As reported in the official edition (DJD 16) and in the Dead Sea Scrolls Bible, the two Proverbs scrolls from Cave 4 preserve parts of chapters 1–2 (4QProv-a) and of chapters 13–15, with a few words of chapter 7 (4QProv-b), and a papyrus from Cave 6 has a few lines of chapter 11. Some lists describe 4QProv-b as containing "31", but the reported contents end at 15:31. No ancient Hebrew manuscript of Proverbs 30–31 older than the medieval codices is known.

deep.title: Claude's theory: Agur's chapter is framed by silence
deep.b: This is my own reading, offered as a suggestion. Agur begins by saying he has no wisdom (30:2–3) and ends by telling the reader to put a hand over his mouth (30:32). Between those points he speaks mostly in questions and riddles, things too wonderful to know (30:18), and he lets the animals teach (30:24–28). The chapter may be built to model the humility it teaches: the sage talks less as he goes, and the last thing he says is how anger is "squeezed" into a fight (30:33). Commentators have noted the link between 30:2–3 and 30:32; the idea that the whole chapter is shaped as a movement from confession to silence is my own.

echoes: Deuteronomy 4:2; Deuteronomy 30:12; Psalm 18:30; 2 Samuel 22:31; Exodus 4:22; Exodus 5:2; Deuteronomy 8:12–14; Exodus 21:17; Genesis 16:4; Genesis 29:31; 1 Kings 4:30–33; Job 38:4–11; Job 40:4; Amos 1:3; Isaiah 7:14; Matthew 6:11; John 3:13; Romans 10:6–7; Revelation 22:18–19

settings.by: Agur son of Jakeh, a sage (perhaps of Massa)
settings.to: Ithiel and Ucal, if those are names; or, if the line is a cry, God himself, with the reader overhearing
settings.when: Unknown. The words come from a sage outside the Solomon collections, placed by the editors near the end of the book
settings.why: Agur admits that he has no wisdom of his own and that no human has climbed to heaven to learn God's secrets. He points instead to God's tested word (30:5) and warns against adding to it (30:6). Knowing that a sage is speaking, in a book of wise sayings, makes the confession striking: wisdom ends by admitting its limits and bowing to revelation.
settings.readers: For the book's later readers, probably in the Persian era when the collection was finished, Agur's words set human wisdom under Scripture. They come just after the long collections of Solomon's proverbs and tell the reader how to hold them: as human wisdom that needs God's word.
views: Agur is a sincere sage confessing the limits of wisdom (most Jewish and Christian readers; Fox, Waltke).
30:1–4 is a doubter's voice, and 30:5–6 an orthodox reply by an editor (a view discussed by Fox and others).
Agur is a pen name of Solomon (Kohelet Rabbah 1:1; Rashi).

settings.when: Spoken as a lifelong request ("before I die")
settings.why: The only prayer in Proverbs asks for two things: to be kept from falsehood, and to be given neither poverty nor riches. Agur explains why: wealth tempts to forget God, poverty to steal and swear falsely. The prayer turns the book's teaching on money into a request to God, and it shows the reader how to pray about daily needs.
settings.readers: If the book was finished in Judah under Persian rule, as many scholars think, its readers lived where some grew rich and many fell into debt (Nehemiah 5). They heard a prayer that warned against both extremes and asked God for daily bread.

settings.by: Agur, if his words run through the chapter; otherwise unnamed sages whose sayings were collected after his
settings.to: A learner, addressed as "you" in 30:10 and 30:32: a young man being trained in wisdom, at home or in a school for scribes and officials
settings.when: No setting is given. The Greek places 30:10–14 with Agur's words and 30:15–33 after 24:34, so the pieces may have had separate origins
settings.why: The sayings train observation. They ask the hearer to notice what is never satisfied, what moves beyond understanding, what overturns order, what small creatures can teach, and what walks with confidence, and then to apply it: do not slander, do not despise parents, do not exalt yourself or stir up anger. The counting form makes them easy to remember and invites the hearer to find what each list shares.
settings.readers: The finished book's readers received these sayings as part of the instruction of the young (1:4), set beside Agur's confession so that close observation of the world went together with humility before God.
views: The whole chapter is Agur's, as its heading suggests (Waltke).
Only 30:1–9 or 30:1–14 is Agur's, and the rest is a separate collection (Fox, Murphy; the Greek order supports a division at 30:14).

title: A Woman of Strength
sum: The last chapter of Proverbs has two parts. First a queen mother speaks: the words of King Lemuel are really his mother's warning to her son not to spend his strength on women or his judgment on wine, and her charge to open his mouth for those who cannot speak (31:1–9). It is the only teaching in the Bible's wisdom books given in a mother's own voice.

Then comes an alphabet poem, twenty-two lines from alef to tav, about the 'eshet chayil, the woman of strength. She works wool and flax, trades like a merchant ship, buys a field, plants a vineyard, feeds her household before dawn, opens her hand to the poor and teaches with wisdom and loyal love. Her husband and sons praise her, and the book that began with "the fear of the LORD" (1:7) ends with "a woman who fears the LORD" (31:30).
readings: The poem describes an ideal wife and mother of a prosperous household, a portrait drawn from life in Israel's towns. It honors women's work in production, trade and management, and in Jewish homes it is sung in praise of the wife and mother. Many Christian readers take her as a model to imitate, though others warn against turning a hymn of praise into a checklist.

The poem completes the book's portrait of Wisdom as a woman. Lady Wisdom built her house and invited the simple in (9:1–6); the woman of strength runs her house and feeds it. She is worth more than red coral, as Wisdom is (3:15; 31:10), and her mouth opens with wisdom (31:26). The young man who has learned to love Wisdom is shown what she looks like in a life (Camp, Yoder).
Read as the church or the soul

From the early church through the Middle Ages most Christian interpreters read her allegorically: the church, bride of Christ, who serves the poor and clothes her children, or Mary, or the faithful soul. Jewish midrash read her as the Torah and as the righteous women of Israel. Most modern readers start from the literal sense but still find in her a picture of wisdom lived out.

views.H: Lemuel is an unknown king, probably not of Israel, and his mother speaks with the authority that queen mothers had in the ancient Near East (1 Kings 2:19). The poem of 31:10–31 has no named author. Its world is a wealthy household with servants, fields, vineyards and trade, where women produced cloth and managed goods. Christine Yoder has argued from its economic terms that it reflects the Persian period (about 500–330 BC), when the book was probably completed.
views.C: Most critics treat 31:1–9 and 31:10–31 as separate pieces, as the Greek order shows: it places 31:1–9 after 30:33 and the poem after 29:27. The poem is a carefully built acrostic, with a mirror pattern near its center (31:19–20) and the heroic style of a song for a warrior (Wolters). Many see the book framed by female figures: Wisdom in chapters 1–9 and the woman of strength at the end.
views.W: Royal instructions are known from Egypt (the Instruction for Merikare, a king's teaching to his son) and Mesopotamia (the Advice to a Prince), but almost all ancient instruction is from father to son. A mother instructing a king is rare. Hymns in praise of a woman's household skill are rarer still. The warnings about wine and the duty to defend the weak match the ideals of ancient kingship, as in Hammurabi's laws.
views.J: Jews read the poem in many ways: as the Torah, as the righteous women of Israel (Midrash Mishlei assigns its verses to Sarah, Rebekah, Leah, Rachel, Miriam, Ruth and others), as the Shekhinah, God's presence, and as the Sabbath. Since the kabbalists, it has been sung at the Friday evening table before Kiddush. The Talmud makes Lemuel Solomon and his mother Bathsheba (Bavli Sanhedrin 70b), and cites 31:6 for the wine given to the condemned (Bavli Sanhedrin 43a).
views.X: Early and medieval Christians read the woman as the church (Augustine, Sermon 37) and later as Mary (Bernard of Clairvaux and others). Since the Reformation she has more often been read as an ideal Christian wife. The Catholic lectionary reads part of the poem on the 33rd Sunday of Ordinary Time in Year A and at Masses for holy women. Today the poem is part of the debate between complementarians and egalitarians about women's roles (see the card below).

deep.h: Lemuel, Massa and a mother's teaching
deep.b:
The heading of 31:1 can be read two ways. Following the Hebrew accents, it says "The words of Lemuel, a king: the oracle with which his mother disciplined him." Joining "king" and massa', it says "Lemuel, king of Massa", an Arabian people descended from Ishmael (Genesis 25:14), the same word that heads Agur's words in 30:1 (see the variant). The Aramaic words in 31:2–3 (bar, "son"; melakhin, "kings") fit a setting east of Israel. Jewish tradition made Lemuel a name for Solomon and his mother Bathsheba, and told how she scolded him on the night he married Pharaoh's daughter, when he slept late on the day the Temple was dedicated (Numbers Rabbah 10:4; Bavli Sanhedrin 70b).

What is certain is that a woman teaches here. The father of chapters 1–9 had told his son to keep "your mother's teaching" (1:8; 6:20), and now the mother's teaching is given. Her three topics are a king's whole duty: guard your strength from many women (31:3), keep your judgment clear of drink (31:4–7), and speak for those who cannot speak for themselves (31:8–9). Many scholars think the poem that follows was placed here so that the mother who warned her son against "women" (31:3) also shows him the one woman worth finding.

Lemuel's mother does not forbid wine to everyone. She forbids it to kings and rulers, because a drunken judge forgets the law and fails the weak (31:4–5). Then she tells her son to give strong drink to the one who is perishing and wine to the bitter in spirit, so they may forget their misery (31:6–7). Some readers take the second command as mercy. The Talmud cites it for the drugged wine given to the condemned (compare Mark 15:23). Others hear a sharp contrast: drink is for those with nothing left to lose, not for those who govern.

The passage stands with other Proverbs warnings (20:1; 23:29–35) and with the Bible's praise of wine as God's gift, "wine that makes people glad at heart" (Psalm 104:15). Whether Christians should drink at all is taken up on the cards at 20:1 and 23:31. This passage raises two narrower questions, set out on the card below. Should leaders abstain even where others need not (compare 1 Timothy 3:3)? And may drink be given to ease suffering?

deep.h: The alphabet of the woman of strength
deep.b:
Each verse of 31:10–31 begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet. The poem cannot be read this way in English, so here are the letters and the first word of each line:

VerseLetterFirst wordMeaning
31:10א alef'eshetA woman of strength
31:11ב betbatachtrusts
31:12ג gimelgemalathushe pays him back
31:13ד daletdareshahshe looks for
31:14ה hehayetahshe has become
31:15ו wawvattaqomshe rises
31:16ז zayinzamemahshe sets her plans
31:17ח chetchagerahshe binds up
31:18ט tetta'amahshe tastes
31:19י yodyadehaher hands
31:20כ kafkappahher palm
31:21ל lamedlo'no (fear)
31:22מ memmarvaddimbedspreads
31:23נ nunnoda'known
31:24ס samekhsadinlinen wraps
31:25ע ayin'ozmight
31:26פ pepihaher mouth
31:27צ tsadetsofiyyahkeeping watch
31:28ק qofqamuthey stand up
31:29ר reshrabbotmany
31:30ש shinsheqera lie
31:31ת tavtenugive

The alphabet frames the woman "from alef to tav", the whole of her. Some letters seem to be chosen for meaning: the tsade line opens with tsofiyyah, which sounds like the Greek sophia, "wisdom" (see the note at 31:27), and the shin and tav lines bring the poem to its climax in the fear of the LORD and public praise. Near the center, 31:19–20 forms a mirror: her hands reach out to the distaff and to the needy. The Greek cannot keep the alphabet, and it puts 31:26 before 31:25, the pe-before-ayin order of Lamentations 2–4.

The phrase 'eshet chayil appears in only one other book. When Ruth comes to Boaz at the threshing floor, he answers: "Now, my daughter, don't be afraid. I will do for you everything you ask, because the whole town knows that you are a woman of worth" (Ruth 3:11). This site translates the phrase "a woman of worth" in Ruth and "a woman of strength" in Proverbs; the Hebrew is the same. In the Leningrad Codex, the base of this translation, Ruth comes right after Proverbs, so a reader of that Bible finishes the poem and meets the woman. The rabbis noticed: Midrash Mishlei assigns 31:29, "you have climbed above them all", to Ruth the Moabite.

The pairing is striking because Ruth is a foreigner, a poor widow who gleans in other people's fields. She has none of the wealth of the household in Proverbs 31. What she has is loyal love (chesed, Ruth 3:10) and courage, and the town's verdict on her is the poem's verdict. Many readers take this as a key to the poem: its heart is not riches or busyness but strength of character and the fear of the LORD (31:30). Boaz himself is a man of chayil (Ruth 2:1), and the people bless him to "do worthy things" with the same phrase as 31:29 (Ruth 4:11).

In many Jewish homes the family sings Eshet Chayil, the whole of 31:10–31, at the Friday evening table before the blessing over wine (Kiddush). The custom began among the kabbalists, the Jewish mystics, who read the woman as the Shekhinah, God's presence, welcomed as bride and queen on the Sabbath. Over time it became a family song in honor of the wife and mother, often sung by the husband and children. Some read it as praise of the Sabbath itself or of the Torah, as Midrash Mishlei did. Its verses have been carved on tombstones. In Sephardi practice, its first verse is recited before the memorial prayer at a woman's funeral.

Modern readers, Jewish and Christian, value the poem as a tribute to women's strength and competence, and some also ask whether one demanding ideal can become a burden for real women. The custom of singing it to the woman of the house answers that worry in its own way: it is praise, offered to a real person at her own table.

For most of Christian history the woman of strength was read as a figure. Augustine preached on her as the church (Sermon 37); medieval writers such as Bernard of Clairvaux saw Mary in her; others, the faithful soul. Since the Reformation, Protestant readers have mostly taken her literally as a model wife, and the Catholic Church reads the poem at Masses for holy women and on the 33rd Sunday of Year A, beside the parable of the talents (Matthew 25:14–30).

Today Christians differ over what she shows about women's roles. Complementarians stress that her many activities serve her household and husband, and that she is praised as a wife and mother. Egalitarians stress that she buys land, runs a business, manages workers, trades with merchants and teaches (31:16, 24, 26), so Scripture does not confine women to private life. Rachel Held Evans argued that the poem is a song of praise, not a to-do list, and borrowed the Jewish blessing "Eshet chayil!" ("Woman of valor!") for women's ordinary acts of courage. Both sides agree that the poem's final praise goes to her fear of the LORD (31:30). The card below sets out how the churches differ.

deep.h: What the poem says, and what it does not
deep.b: The poem is often taken to describe what a woman should do. It is more exactly a hymn of praise: it begins with a question about how rare she is (31:10) and ends by calling the community to honor her (31:31). It says nothing about her husband ruling her; he "trusts" her (31:11), sits at the gate while she works (31:23), and praises her (31:28–29). It also says nothing about beauty, except that it does not last (31:30). It does assume a household with servants and land, so it describes a woman of some means. Readers should not turn a portrait of one exceptional woman into a list of duties for all, nor overlook that the book written for young men (1:4) ends by teaching them to value such a woman above anything they could buy.

echoes: Ruth 3:11; Ruth 2:1; Ruth 4:11; 12:4; 1:7; 9:1–6; 3:13–15; 8:11; Deuteronomy 17:17; 1 Kings 11:3; 1 Kings 2:19; Psalm 72:1–4; Psalm 104:15; Psalm 34:8; Psalm 112:1; Genesis 30:13; Mark 15:23; Luke 1:48; 1 Peter 3:3–4; 1 Timothy 3:3

settings.what: A queen mother's instruction to her son
settings.when: Unknown; the heading presents it as teaching she gave him, perhaps as he came to the throne
settings.why: She warns him against the two classic ruins of kings, many women and much drink, because both cost a ruler his strength and judgment. Then she gives him his task: to speak for the voiceless and judge the poor fairly. Knowing that a mother speaks changes the tone. These are not a scribe's maxims but a parent's urgent plea ("What, my son?"), and they show a woman as the bearer of wisdom to a king.
settings.readers: The book's readers, many of them young men being trained for life and service, heard a woman's voice teaching the book's final lessons about justice, and were reminded that their own mothers' teaching counted (1:8).
views: Lemuel was a king of Massa or another people east of Israel, and his mother a royal teacher (Fox, Clifford).
Lemuel is Solomon and his mother Bathsheba (Bavli Sanhedrin 70b; Numbers Rabbah 10:4).

settings.what: The poem of the woman of strength
settings.by: An unnamed poet; some think the poem continues the words of Lemuel's mother
settings.to: Young men who will choose wives, and the whole community, called to praise her in the gates (31:31)
settings.when: No setting is given. It closes the book, perhaps added by its final editors
settings.why: The poem praises a woman who embodies wisdom in daily life: hard work, shrewd trade, generosity to the poor, wise teaching and the fear of the LORD. For a young man, it shows what to value in a wife, not charm or beauty but strength and faith. For the community, it calls for her work to be honored in public. If Lemuel's mother speaks it, she answers her own warning in 31:3 with a picture of the wife a king should seek.
settings.readers: For the finished book's readers, the poem tied the whole collection together: Lady Wisdom of chapters 1–9 and the fear of the LORD of 1:7 return as a living woman. Later Jewish readers sang it on the Sabbath, and Christians read it of the church and of the godly woman.
views: A portrait of the ideal wife and mother (most readers).
Wisdom in human form, closing the book's frame (Camp, Yoder).
A song in the style of a warrior's praise, celebrating a woman's heroism in ordinary life (Wolters).

traditions.q: Lemuel's mother forbids drink to rulers but tells her son to give it to the perishing (31:4–7). Should leaders abstain even where others need not, and may drink be given to ease suffering?
views: No special rule of abstinence for leaders: all are bound by temperance, which avoids every excess of food and alcohol (Catechism 2290). Easing the pain of the dying is a mercy, and painkillers may be used even at the risk of shortening life, if death is not intended (Catechism 2279).

Clergy are held to sobriety, not abstinence. The Apostolic Canons tell a bishop, priest or deacon given to drink to stop or be deposed (Canon 42). Wine is used in the Eucharist and given up on many fast days.
No rule beyond Scripture's own: an overseer must not be a drunkard (1 Timothy 3:3). Drinking is a Christian freedom for leaders and members alike, and wine is used in the Lord's Supper.

No rule of abstinence for clergy or laity, and wine is used at Holy Communion. In the 1800s the Church of England Temperance Society welcomed both abstainers and the moderate, treating abstinence as a personal choice.

Leaders must not be given to drink, but abstinence is a freedom, not a law. Calvin taught that God gave wine not only for need but to gladden the heart, to be used with thanks and moderation (Institutes 3.10.2). Some Reformed churches have urged their officers to abstain for the sake of others.

Historically abstinence, with room for real need. Wesley's General Rules (1743) forbade drinking spirits "unless in cases of extreme necessity", which allowed the medicinal use that 31:6 describes. American Methodists later led the temperance movement and brought in grape juice for communion.

Many say leaders should abstain. The Southern Baptist Convention's 2006 resolution opposed drinking alcohol and urged that no one who drinks be elected to its boards or committees, a rule for leaders like the one in 31:4. Many other Baptists leave drinking to conscience.

Abstinence for all. The Assemblies of God position paper (2016) urges total abstinence. It cites 31:4–7, extends the warning from rulers to every believer, and stresses the leader's example (1 Timothy 3:3).

traditions.q: The woman of strength buys land, trades, manages workers and teaches (31:16–26). Does she show a pattern for women's roles in the home, the church and public life?
views: Man and woman are equal in dignity (Catechism 369–372). The Church uses the poem to honor holy women and women's work in family and society: it is read at Masses for holy women and on the 33rd Sunday of Year A, beside the parable of the talents.

The priesthood is kept for men. Women have served as deaconesses in the early and Byzantine church, and some women saints bear the title "equal to the apostles". The church honors women's work in the home and beyond without making this poem a rule for church office.

Divided. The Evangelical Lutheran Church in America, whose parent bodies began ordaining women in 1970, sees in her a capable leader. The Lutheran Church–Missouri Synod keeps the pastoral office for men and praises her as a model of a woman's service in home, church and society.

Divided. The Presbyterian Church in America keeps ordained office for men, and many of its teachers share the complementarian Danvers Statement (1987), which affirms distinct roles for men and women in home and church. The Presbyterian Church (U.S.A.) ordains women as elders and ministers. Egalitarians, whose statement Men, Women and Biblical Equality (1989) affirms shared leadership, point to her property, trade and teaching.
The United Methodist Church has given women full clergy rights since 1956. On that view a capable woman who trades, manages and teaches is a model for women's leadership, not an exception.

The Baptist Faith and Message (2000) teaches that a wife is to submit graciously to her husband's servant leadership and to serve as his helper in managing the household and nurturing the next generation (article 18). It limits the office of pastor to men (article 6). Southern Baptist teachers often present the woman of Proverbs 31 as a model of that calling. Other Baptist bodies, such as American Baptist Churches USA, ordain women.

The Assemblies of God holds that Scripture does not bar women from any ministry and has ordained women since 1935 (The Role of Women in Ministry). On that view a capable, teaching woman like this one fits the Spirit's gifts to daughters as well as sons (Joel 2:28).
